AI From Zero

How a small team in Pune built a privacy guard, and learned how AI products are really made

1

The problem worth solving

Anaya notices something odd in the chat, and learns how a product person decides what to build, and what to leave alone.

  1. 1The Number in the ChatA product manager finds identity numbers in a week of customer chats and must decide whether the finding deserves a year of work. The chapter introduces personal data, counting before deciding, choosing between problems, and the written decision.9 min read✓ read
  2. 2Four Questions Before BuildingAn engineer asks the question every idea should survive, and a feature nobody noticed teaches the team where products really fail.9 min read✓ read
  3. 3Asking About YesterdayFive conversations teach a product manager that the useful question is never "would you like this?", and that the problem was not quite where she thought it was.10 min read✓ read
  4. 4Who Else Is Standing HereA compliance head gives a conditional yes, and a product manager learns to size a market from the bottom up and to take the competition she cannot see as seriously as the competition she can.8 min read✓ read
  5. 5Choosing What Not to DoOn a Sunday call a retired teacher asks the question that turns a pile of good ideas into a strategy, and a product acquires its name.8 min read✓ read
  6. 6A Plan Others Can BelieveA strategy is only a sentence until other people can act on it. Anaya learns to promise outcomes instead of dates, to list who can say no, and to imagine the project already dead.9 min read✓ read
  7. 7Writing It Down So Others Can Build ItAn engineer draws the guard on a napkin, a product manager turns it into a specification a stranger could build from, and a support agent shows what a paper mock-up can find that a meeting cannot.9 min read✓ read
2

Meeting the machine

What a language model is, how to talk to it, and how to tell whether it did well.

  1. 8What the Machine IsOn a Sunday call a product manager admits she cannot say what "powered by AI" means, and a retired linguist and an engineer between them build the answer, one plain idea at a time.8 min read✓ read
  2. 9The First ConversationAn engineer lets the product manager watch a message go to a model and come back, and what she sees on the receipt matters as much as what she reads in the answer.7 min read✓ read
  3. 10A Mind With No MemoryA sweet-shop owner who remembers every regular teaches a product manager why a chatbot does not, and what the difference does to her bill and to her problem.6 min read✓ read
  4. 11Giving InstructionsThe team asks a model to do the guard's job for the first time, watches it be wrong in three different ways, and learns the difference between making a failure rarer and removing its cause.8 min read✓ read
  5. 12Knowing Whether It WorksThe team stops trusting how an answer feels, writes the correct answers down before looking at the tool's, and discovers that the version everyone liked was not the best one.7 min read✓ read
  6. 13Sorting and SummarisingOne job with a right answer and one without. The team measures a sorter, finds the failure its single score was hiding, and then checks a summary for the thing it left out.7 min read✓ read
3

Finding things, and the whole machine

Long documents, search by words and by meaning, and how the parts join into one working system.

  1. 14Too Long to Read at OnceTo understand how the chatbot answers questions from Sahaj's own documents, a product manager cuts a policy into pieces with scissors, three times, and learns that no way of cutting is right.7 min read✓ read
  2. 15Finding by WordsA product manager plays the part of the search box, learns why the oldest way of finding things fails the customers who most need help, and why it is still exactly right for an identity number.6 min read✓ read
  3. 16Finding by MeaningA bazaar where stalls of the same trade stand in the same lane gives a product manager the picture she needs for the idea that rescued search, and a number to be suspicious of.7 min read✓ read
  4. 17How Good Is GoodSomeone senior asks the question every AI project eventually meets. The answer is two numbers, a choice between them that is not an engineer's to make, and an uncomfortable look at a figure Anaya had quoted without checking.7 min read✓ read
  5. 18The Whole MachineEvery part has now been built and broken by hand, so the whole chatbot can be drawn from memory, named, and followed by a compliance head with a red pen who wants to know where each word goes.7 min read✓ read
  6. 19Answers a Program Can UseA paragraph is fine for a person and useless to a program. The team learns why "reply in JSON, please" is not good enough, and how to design a form so well that the model has no room to make things up.7 min read✓ read
4

Giving it work to do

Tools, thinking models, hostile text, grading at scale, and what it all costs.

  1. 20Giving the Machine HandsA twelve-digit order number looks exactly like an Aadhaar number, and the only way to tell them apart is to look it up. Letting a model do the looking teaches the team what a loop is, what one costs, and which of its actions need a human.7 min read✓ read
  2. 21Long Windows, Careful RoomsA salesman announces that a very large context window makes all this effort unnecessary, and a product manager asks him the one question that ends the meeting. What goes in the room matters more than how big it is.7 min read✓ read
  3. 22Machines That Think FirstA model that works out its answer before giving it gets the hard cases right and takes eleven seconds to do so. Between a train that stopped near Lonavala and a chat window that cannot wait, the team learns when thinking is worth buying and how to make a wait bearable.7 min read✓ read
  4. 23Searching BetterA customer is quoted last year's late fee, and four improvements to search, each measured against the same answer key, show that the dullest one is the only one that can promise anything.7 min read✓ read
  5. 24When the Page Gives OrdersThe guard exists to read what strangers write, which makes it the most exposed program in the building. The team tests its tenth sentence, watches a model obey a stranger, and learns the difference between a defence that lowers odds and one that removes a power.8 min read✓ read
  6. 25Grading a Thousand AnswersHand-checking stops working at about fifty answers. The team puts a machine on the marking, checks the marker before trusting it, and then does the most useful thing in the field, which needs no machine at all.7 min read✓ read
  7. 26What It Really Costs"It depends on tokens" is not an answer to a finance director. A product manager prices the guard properly, finds three very different totals for the same tool, and sees why the order in which her four boxes run is the cheapest design decision she will make.8 min read✓ read
5

The messy real world

Scans and photographs, what you may send, the rules, a spec for a thing that varies, and designing for the wrong answer.

  1. 27Paper, Photos and ScansUntil now every sentence the guard read was already text. A random sample of fifty attachments shows how seldom that is true of real life, and how a capital O pretending to be a zero can walk a number straight past a rule.7 min read✓ read
  2. 28What You May SendEverything so far assumed the text could be sent. Lakshmi puts three documents on a table, asks three questions in a fixed order, and a vendor's terms of service turn out to say things nobody had read.7 min read✓ read
  3. 29Rules, Risk and ResponsibilityLakshmi explains what twenty years in a bank taught her about paperwork, and the team writes the one-page document that says what the guard is for, what it gets wrong, and what it must never be used to do. Then they try to delete one customer, and find where she lives.9 min read✓ read
  4. 30The Spec for a Thing That VariesA thirty-day notice that a model is being retired shows what a specification for software that does not behave the same way twice must actually contain, and what a switch for turning the AI off should leave running.8 min read✓ read
  5. 31Build, Buy or Teach ItA vendor offers to sell the team what it has spent six months building, and a founder offers to make a model of their own. Both proposals sound sensible, and each has to survive the same test.9 min read✓ read
  6. 32Designing for the Wrong AnswerAt ninety percent, one answer in ten is wrong, and what the screen does about that one decides whether the tool is trusted. Then a pilot that was designed to be able to fail does something stranger: it succeeds, and nothing changes.8 min read✓ read
6

Under the hood

The plumbing, choosing a model, retrieval that survives review, agents, voices and pictures, release gates, and assuming the worst.

  1. 33The Plumbing Under the MagicA two-hour outage in which nothing raised an error persuades a product manager that she needs to understand, at the level of a plumber's diagram, the ordinary software around the one unpredictable part.8 min read✓ read
  2. 34Choosing a Model on Your Own CasesA founder wants to switch to whichever model topped last week's chart. The team does what you do with a car, takes three of them for a drive on their own roads, and then learns to say exactly what is in the room each model walks into.8 min read✓ read
  3. 35Retrieval That Survives a ReviewA prototype works because you chose every document and you are the only user. Production removes both comforts. Four questions that fit every retrieval system are put to the chatbot in a room full of people who would like it to fail.8 min read✓ read
  4. 36Workflows, Agents and the Standard PlugA bank teller can look up your balance but cannot send your money on your word. Three questions about the support console, how much to let a model decide, how to stop it, and what a standard plug does and does not promise, are settled by crossing things out.8 min read✓ read
  5. 37Pages, Pictures and VoicesRead a railway timetable aloud word by word and nobody learns when the train leaves. The team takes on photographs and voice notes at last, finds the stage at which meaning first goes wrong, and builds a test that can tell a hearing mistake from a thinking one.7 min read✓ read
  6. 38Gates, Traces and RollbacksOne edit to one instruction, made on a Friday night without a test, shows why a change that does not feel like a deployment must pass through a gate; and why, afterwards, you need to be able to answer "why did it do that?" in forty seconds.7 min read✓ read
  7. 39Assuming the WorstA compliance report, a Saturday spent trying to break the thing with sweets as prizes, and a table in which every safeguard sits next to the test that proves it. The model will be manipulated; everything around it is the defence.8 min read✓ read
7

A real product, and a job

Shipping it, pricing it, growing it, counting it, running it with real users, and getting hired to do it.

  1. 40A Product, Not a DemoA dish you cook well for two people is not an item on a restaurant menu. Before the festival season, the team lists everything that stands between a working prototype and a service, and writes down, for each big decision, what would make them reverse it.7 min read✓ read
  2. 41Shipping the Whole ThingIn December, Anaya stands in front of the people who doubted the idea and tells them what she built, what broke, who used it, what it costs, and what she does not know. The eleven stages she followed are the year she has just lived, with names.8 min read✓ read
  3. 42Who Pays, and How MuchA lender's technical lead asks what the guard would cost him, and a product manager finds that the answer to the question depends on three different people, four ways of charging, and a row in a table that most price lists never draw.8 min read✓ read
  4. 43How People Find It and StayA tool that nobody finds protects nobody. Five developers are handed a README and nothing else, a stopwatch records where they give up, and a spelling checker teaches a product manager where the first moment of value must happen.7 min read✓ read
  5. 44Counting What MattersOnce real people use the tool, the question changes from "does it work?" to "what do they do?", and a privacy product has to answer it without recording a single thing it exists to hide. A sample-size sum then explains why a young company cannot run the test it wants.7 min read✓ read
  6. 45The Tools and the HarnessA new engineer asks which tool is for what, and an old engineer answers with a drawing of slots and not a list of brands. Then the same engineer is given a weekly report to build twice, once with fixed steps and once with an agent, and the two are measured against the same twenty weeks.12 min read✓ read
  7. 46Real People, Real UseA demonstration works while you are watching it. A product has to work when nobody is, for people who owe you nothing. In the spring Anaya prepares the guard for strangers, recruits them honestly, sits on her hands while they use it, and ships one change because of what she saw.9 min read✓ read
  8. 47The Work, and the JobA former bank analyst has built something real and has no idea how to show it. Over a few Sunday evenings Anaya helps her turn a year of work into a picture of the jobs she wants, a page of evidence, and a rehearsed way of answering the questions that decide whether she gets them.9 min read✓ read
